articles.title: I built FoxIO's 54 KB HTTP/3 accordion by hand. aioquic's decoder unfolded it to 200 MB.
articles.excerpt: On October 20, FoxIO disclosed "Header Accordions": a class of QPACK amplification attacks against HTTP/3 servers. QPACK is HTTP/3's header compression. The bug pattern is simple to state — implementa…
articles.body: On October 20, FoxIO disclosed "Header Accordions": a class of QPACK amplification attacks against HTTP/3 servers. QPACK is HTTP/3's header compression. The bug pattern is simple to state — implementations cap the size of the compressed header block that arrives on the wire, but not the size of what it expands into when decoded. Seven of the ten stacks FoxIO tested were vulnerable. quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, lsquic, and Wireshark have fixes. Three had none at disclosure: Bun, the Rust h3 crate, and aioquic — the Python QUIC/HTTP/3 library, which also means mitmproxy's HTTP/3 path. FoxIO's worst number was ~4,000x amplification on Bun.
articles.author: frank chu

articles.title: EKS 1.37 Upgrade Checklist: What Breaks and How to Test It
articles.excerpt: Seven changes that break Amazon EKS clusters going from 1.36 to 1.37, with a test command for each. By Evgeny Anikiev, AWS-certified DevOps engineer with 10+ years running build automation, CI/CD, and…
articles.body: Seven changes that break Amazon EKS clusters going from 1.36 to 1.37, with a test command for each. By Evgeny Anikiev, AWS-certified DevOps engineer with 10+ years running build automation, CI/CD, and Kubernetes in production. Last verified: October 22, 2026, against the Amazon EKS 1.37 documentation. TL;DR: Amazon EKS has supported Kubernetes 1.37 since October 2, 2026. Most of the release is additive, but seven changes can break running workloads. Test each one with the command in its section, rehearse on a staging cluster, then upgrade the control plane, add-ons, and nodes in that order. The seven changes: SELinux mount labeling is on by default. Static pods can no longer reference Secrets or ConfigMaps. The kubelet refuses to start with deprecated cAdvisor flags.

articles.title: Meet Ovis: a compiler that reads plain English
articles.excerpt: Everything starts with a small thought, what if I merge LLM & LLVM? Will I able to write English Pseudo-code with the performance of a compiled language? Ovis is a programming language whose source co…
articles.body: Everything starts with a small thought, what if I merge LLM & LLVM? Will I able to write English Pseudo-code with the performance of a compiled language? English in, native code out Ovis is a programming language whose source code is plain English, compiled through LLVM into a native executable. You write lines the way you would say them, such as show the average of numbers rounded to 2 decimals , and get a fast binary that can call any C library. The twist is how it reads English. A deterministic parser reads every line. A small language model built into the compiler steps in only when a line is unclear, and even then it never writes code: it picks one of the readings that already type-check. Every choice it makes is written down, so the next build needs no model at all.

articles.body: I can spend a week probing your firewall and find nothing. Or I can call your front desk, sound confident, and have someone reset a password for me in four minutes. Guess which one attackers reach for first. The hardest system to patch is not your server. It is the person who answers the phone. The weakest link has always been human Kevin Mitnick was once the most wanted computer criminal in America. He was arrested in 1995, he did his time, and then he spent the rest of his life, until he died in 2023, as a security consultant teaching companies how he had done it. Here is the thing people miss about Mitnick. He was a skilled technician, but his favorite tool was a telephone.

articles.body: Threat modeling is frequently cited as the most cost-effective security activity in software engineering. Fixing a structural authorization flaw during design costs a fraction of refactoring a production database or remediating a public data breach. Yet in fast-moving engineering organizations, traditional threat modeling often fails. Multi-week architectural reviews create bottlenecks, resulting in developers bypassing security reviews to meet sprint deadlines. To make threat modeling sustainable, it must be lightweight, developer-centric, and embedded directly into Agile ceremonies .

articles.title: Australia's bizarre 'Spider Crater' seen from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 22, 2026
articles.excerpt: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia.
articles.body: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one. What is it? One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said . In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape.

articles.title: Durability tests reveal how the iPhone Duo handles thousands of continuous folds

articles.body: Credit: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority TL;DR Automated stress tests by YouTuber Tim Pan (10,500 folds plus sub-zero testing) and Joanna Stern (over 32,000 folds) show that the iPhone Duo’s 3D-printed titanium hinge remains sturdy and smooth all throughout. However, continuous folding significantly deepens the inner display crease, both visually and to the touch. Other iPhone Duo quirks include single-sided NFC positioning, lack of an internal earpiece (forcing speakerphone when open), minor thermal throttling, and UI misfires when opened slowly. Apple spent years watching Android OEMs pioneer the foldable landscape, and then made deliberate design choices to ensure its first folding iPhone wouldn’t suffer from the same teething issues as early Galaxy Fold generations.

articles.title: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community
articles.excerpt: NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall.
articles.body: Dear NASA Science Community, NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), and answer your questions. ( Details below. ) We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. This has often come with contract management challenges, unpredictability, and not enough funding. NASA is committed to doing better — and I’m excited to share with you how we’re making it happen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.
